title: Autonomization Of Quantum Systems And The Emergence Of The Work Operator
authors: Carlo Cepollaro, Danial Chughtai, Alberto Spalvieri, Marcus Huber, Alberto Rolandi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20602v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimation of work at the quantum scale remains a central challenge in quantum thermodynamics. Canonical approaches have a fundamental drawback: they assume classical control of the quantum system, as implicit in a time-dependent Hamiltonian. Yet the energetic cost of implementing this control is omitted and can exceed the system's energy scale by orders of magnitude, calling into question the operational significance of work values. We address this by autonomizing the controlled energy transfer, embedding the driven dynamics into an energy-conserving evolution on a larger quantum system. Work is then unambiguously identified with the energy transferred between the two systems, singling out a unique observable on the driven system: the work operator. We show that the quantum work operator evades a no-go theorem by deriving a quantum fluctuation theorem that recovers the Jarzynski equality in classical scenarios. We incorporate imperfect control and quantify corrections to work statistics. Extending the framework to open quantum systems, we obtain an operatorial first law in which work, heat, and internal-energy changes are represented by distinct operators on the reduced system. Together, these results settle the long-standing debate over whether work is a quantum observable: it is, once the controlling system is included in the description rather than treated as external.
tldr: This paper resolves the long-standing debate on whether work is a quantum observable by autonomizing the controlled energy transfer and deriving a work operator that satisfies a quantum fluctuation theorem.
motivation: Standard approaches to quantum work assume classical control, ignoring the energetic cost of control, which can be orders of magnitude larger than the system's energy scale. This undermines the operational significance of work values.
method: The authors embed the driven dynamics into an energy-conserving evolution on a larger quantum system, autonomizing the controlled energy transfer. They identify work as the energy transferred between the two systems, defining a unique work operator on the driven system.
result: They derive a quantum fluctuation theorem that recovers the Jarzynski equality in classical scenarios, incorporate imperfect control, and extend the framework to open quantum systems, obtaining an operatorial first law with distinct work, heat, and internal-energy operators.
conclusion: Work is a quantum observable once the controlling system is included in the description, settling the debate and providing a rigorous foundation for quantum thermodynamics.

title: Hi-qdc: An Isometric Modular Scalable Architecture For Quantum Data Centers
authors: Mohadeseh Azari, Anoosha Fayyaz, Amy Babay, David Tipper, Prashant Krishnamurthy, Kaushik Seshadreesan
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20633v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Server-centric quantum data-center architectures offer scalability by distributing communication tasks across QPUs rather than concentrating complexity in a centralized switching core. However, scaling such architectures increases the path length, the number of Bell-state measurements, and the loss of end-to-end fidelity. We ask whether the path diversity of a server-centric topology can be converted into a mechanism for preserving not only rate, but also fidelity. We study this through end-to-end purification as a fidelity-restoration mechanism. First, in a black-box model, we determine the minimum number of raw end-to-end Werner-state copies, each carrying the degraded Werner parameter of a distance-ell path, that purification must consume to recover a single copy matching an elementary link, comparing recursive 2-to-1 and optimized nested r-to-1 purification. Second, we instantiate these requirements in a probabilistic BCube architecture, whose edge-disjoint path diversity supplies the raw copies. Because purification imposes a lower bound on input fidelity, no path redundancy can raise the output below this threshold, which limits scaling. To address it we present the Hop-Independent Quantum Data Center (HI-QDC), an isometric, modular, scalable architecture in which purification transforms end-to-end entanglement across a module into an effective link-level resource for the inter-module topology. Our results identify the regimes in which a BCube module, under end-to-end purification, preserves both the fidelity and the yield of an elementary link. The module then hides its internal hop count and acts as an effective elementary link for a higher-level network. Thus topology supplies the path multiplicity purification requires, while purification converts it into fidelity recovery, enabling recursively scalable quantum data-center networks.
tldr: This paper proposes a modular, isometric quantum data center architecture (HI-QDC) that uses path diversity and end-to-end purification to preserve fidelity and rate, enabling scalable quantum networks.
motivation: Server-centric quantum data centers face scalability challenges due to increased path length and fidelity loss; the authors aim to convert path diversity into a fidelity-preserving mechanism.
method: The authors analyze end-to-end purification in a black-box model and instantiate it in a probabilistic BCube architecture, then propose HI-QDC where purification transforms intra-module entanglement into effective link-level resources for inter-module scaling.
result: They identify regimes where a BCube module preserves both fidelity and yield of an elementary link, effectively hiding internal hop count and acting as an elementary link for higher-level networks.
conclusion: The HI-QDC architecture enables recursively scalable quantum data center networks by combining topology-provided path multiplicity with purification-based fidelity recovery.

title: Fermionic Genuine Multiparty Entanglement
authors: James Allen, Liuke Lyu, William Witczak-Krempa
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20707v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement can show fundamentally different behavior in fermionic systems. However, while bipartite measures of fermionic entanglement have been established, genuine multiparty entanglement (GME) in fermionic systems is much less understood. We introduce an efficiently computable measure (via semi-definite programming) of fermionic GME, fermion genuine multiparty negativity (fGMN), and show that it is an entanglement monotone and a natural multipartite extension of the fermionic negativity. Using this measure, we find many states which have fGMN but no non-fermionic GME, including large classes of fermionic stabilizer states. The fGMN also displays some major phenomenological differences to the bipartite fermionic negativity, such as finite sudden death points over separation and temperature.
tldr: Introduces a computable measure of genuine multiparty entanglement for fermionic systems, revealing states with fermionic GME but no non-fermionic GME.
motivation: Genuine multiparty entanglement in fermionic systems is poorly understood despite established bipartite measures.
method: Defines fermion genuine multiparty negativity (fGMN) via semi-definite programming and proves it is an entanglement monotone.
result: fGMN detects GME in many fermionic stabilizer states that lack non-fermionic GME, and exhibits sudden death behavior.
conclusion: fGMN provides a practical tool for studying multipartite fermionic entanglement with qualitatively different behavior from bipartite measures.

They demonstrate that fGMN can be efficiently computed via semi-definite programming (SDP). Additionally, they show that fGMN exhibits finite sudden death points as a function of separation and temperature, contrasting with the behavior of bipartite fermionic negativity.

title: Hardness And Complexity Transition Of Noisy Random Circuit Sampling
authors: Byeongseon Go, Changhun Oh, Hyunseok Jeong
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Random circuit sampling (RCS) is a leading candidate for demonstrating quantum advantage, supported by strong complexity-theoretic evidence of hardness in the ideal setting and by rapid experimental progress to date. In practice, however, noise is unavoidable, and a central problem is to identify the noise-strength boundary between classically simulable and classically hard regimes. In this work, we establish an architecture-general hardness bound for this boundary for the standard local depolarizing noise of strength [MATH]. Assuming the standard average-case #P-hardness conjecture for ideal RCS, we show that, for any circuit architecture satisfying this conjecture, noisy RCS on the same architecture remains hard to simulate classically within any inverse-polynomial total variation distance whenever [MATH] for [MATH]-qubit circuits of depth [MATH], unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses. Crucially, noisy-RCS hardness follows without any additional conjectural or architecture-specific assumption beyond those already entering the ideal-RCS hardness framework. Our proof combines a low-degree polynomial extrapolation with a monotonicity reduction showing that efficient classical simulation at one depolarizing noise strength implies efficient simulation at every larger strength. Together, these ingredients transfer the standard ideal-RCS hardness conjecture to sampling hardness at a prespecified noise strength. Finally, combining the convergence-to-uniformity result of Dalzell et al. [Commun. Math. Phys. 405, 78 (2024)] with our monotonicity reduction yields efficient classical simulation for [MATH] on layered, regularly connected architectures. Thus, wherever the two architectural settings overlap, this identifies [MATH] as the asymptotic complexity-transition scale.
tldr: Establishes a rigorous hardness bound for noisy random circuit sampling under local depolarizing noise, identifying the noise strength threshold for classical simulability.
motivation: Noise in random circuit sampling experiments threatens the classical hardness that underpins quantum advantage claims; a precise noise boundary is needed to understand when classical simulation becomes feasible.
method: Combines low-degree polynomial extrapolation with a monotonicity reduction to transfer the ideal-RCS hardness conjecture to noisy settings, and uses convergence-to-uniformity results to identify the transition scale.
result: Proves that noisy RCS remains hard for noise strength p < O(1/(nD)) under standard conjectures, and becomes classically simulable for p > O(1/(nD)) on layered architectures.
conclusion: Provides the first architecture-general hardness bound for noisy RCS, clarifying the complexity transition and guiding experimental demonstrations of quantum advantage.

The proof combines a low-degree polynomial extrapolation technique with a monotonicity reduction showing that efficient classical simulation at one noise strength implies efficient simulation at any larger strength. This transfers the ideal hardness conjecture to a specific noise regime. Conversely, using a convergence-to-uniformity result from Dalzell et al., they show that for layered, regularly connected architectures, efficient classical simulation is possible when γ = ω(log n/(nd)). title: A Quantum Interface Between Neutral-Atoms And Trapped-Ions Quantum Registers
authors: Ayelet Hasson, Gal Dekel, Ehud Shahar, Nitzan Akerman, Roee Ozeri
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid quantum systems combining neutral atoms and trapped ions offer the prospect of integrating the scalability of atom arrays with the high-fidelity control available in trapped-ion platforms. Here we propose and analyze a quantum interface between individually trapped neutral atoms and a trapped-ion crystal. In our scheme, a neutral 88Sr atom trapped in optical tweezers interacts with a small 88Sr+ ion crystal, and by exciting the atom to a Rydberg state, the atom-ion polarization interaction is strongly enhanced, resulting in a state-dependent modification of the ions' collective motional modes. We show that this shift enables conditional control of a MS gate, allowing the neutral atom to act as a control qubit for an entangling operation between two ions. We investigate the feasibility of the scheme by analyzing Rydberg trapping in the combined optical tweezers and Paul trap potentials, identifying negative-polarizability Rydberg states as particularly favorable for stable confinement. We further evaluate the relevant trapping conditions, Rydberg lifetimes, and coherence requirements, and show that the proposed interface is compatible with realistic experimental parameters. These results establish a practical route toward deterministic atom-ion hybrid quantum gates and quantum interfaces.
tldr: Proposes a quantum interface between neutral atoms and trapped ions using Rydberg-enhanced atom-ion interactions to enable entangling gates.
motivation: Combining neutral atoms and trapped ions could leverage the scalability of atom arrays and high-fidelity control of ions, but a practical interface is missing.
method: A neutral 88Sr atom in optical tweezers is excited to a Rydberg state, enhancing polarization interaction with a 88Sr+ ion crystal, enabling state-dependent control of collective motional modes for a Molmer-Sorensen gate.
result: The scheme is feasible with realistic parameters, using negative-polarizability Rydberg states for stable confinement, and achieves conditional entangling operations.
conclusion: This work establishes a practical route toward deterministic atom-ion hybrid quantum gates and interfaces.

abstract: ArXiv:2607.21093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-evolving entangled states describe quantum particles whose correlations evolve in time according to a well-defined dynamics. Such states can be generated in a variety of physical systems and are promising resources for several quantum technologies, ranging from quantum clock synchronization to quantum communication. However, their full potential is currently limited by the fact that the entanglement dynamics often occur on timescales comparable to the achievable synchronization precision, especially in experiments aimed at distributing entanglement through noisy urban channels. Our results demonstrate that time-evolving entanglement can be reliably transmitted through a noisy urban free-space channel, representing an important benchmark toward long-distance free-space quantum communication and the future implementation of time-correlated entangled states in demanding scenarios such as satellite-based quantum networks.

title: Discrete-modulated Continuous-variable Quantum Key Distribution With Uncertainty Principle

abstract: ArXiv:2607.20840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution is a compelling framework for scalable quantum networks due to its seamless integration with existing optical communication infrastructure. abstract: ArXiv:2607.20623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning compact, interpretable descriptions of quantum many-body states is an important task in quantum science. Given access to quantum copies, we prove this can be accomplished with [MATH] copies of [MATH]. We also show that above a fidelity of [MATH] any stationary point is the unique global maximum while below [MATH] the optimization landscape can have spurious stationary points, and hence [MATH] marks a transition point in the optimization landscape for this problem. title: Unitary $k$-designs Without Hamiltonian Quenches
authors: Pratik Nandy
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unitary designs provide an efficient means of emulating Haar randomness without the requirement of exponential resources. Hamiltonian quench protocols have recently been shown to generate such designs, but achieving this typically requires multiple independent Hamiltonian quenches, even via temporal ensembles. Here, we show that no Hamiltonian quenches are required: a single chaotic Hamiltonian is sufficient to generate approximate unitary [MATH]-designs. We introduce a two-Pauli-kick (2PK) protocol, where unitary evolution under a fixed Hamiltonian is interspersed with two Pauli operator insertions (kicks). By evaluating the frame potential, we demonstrate that the resulting ensemble converges to the Haar value, indicating the emergence of approximate unitary designs. We verify this protocol for Gaussian random matrix ensembles, the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model, and simplified spin (bosonic) SYK models. Furthermore, our protocol admits a canonical definition of finite-temperature frame potentials and establishes the relation with the partition function. We outline a plausible holographic interpretation of our protocol from the dual gravity picture.

title: Finite Key Underwater Quantum Key Distribution: Performance Analysis And Improvements
authors: Trevor Thomas, Michael Warnock, Sarah Previte, Benjamin Drozdenko, Walter O. Krawec
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) allows for the establishment of a secret key between two parties, secure against computationally unbounded adversaries. Most experimental and theoretical research in this area, investigates the performance of QKD over fiber or free space channels. A growing body of work, however, has begun to investigate its performance in underwater scenarios. Here, we consider the realistic finite key scenario, and evaluate the simulated performance of two different decoy state protocols. We show that there are certain underwater channels where "simpler" QKD protocols outperform more complex ones. Finally, we also investigate methods to improve QKD performance underwater, specifically looking at classical advantage distillation, which we show can greatly improve the maximal distance supported by QKD underwater.

title: Component-Level Inverse Design Of Transmon Qubits Using Neural Networks
authors: Olivia Seidel, Firas Abouzahr, Abhishek Chakraborty, Sadman Ahmed Shanto, Saikat Das, Daniel Baxter, Jonathan Asaadi, Nicola Pancotti, Haoyu Yang, Brucek Khailany, Sara Sussman, Enectali Figueroa-Feliciano, Eli M Levenson-Falk, Taylor L. Patti
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Designing a superconducting qubit to realize specific Hamiltonian parameters typically requires iterating through a time and compute-intensive forward loop in which the designer chooses a layout geometry, simulates it, extracts circuit parameters such as capacitances, and refines the geometry. We study the inverse version of this task using a neural-network workflow that maps target Hamiltonian parameters directly to component-level layout parameters, which we subsequently demonstrate on a planar transmon layout. During training, we pair the inverse model with a frozen forward surrogate model and evaluate the loss in Hamiltonian space rather than in layout-parameter space. In validation against a conventional EM solver, 97% of generated designs produce usable geometries, and the inverse-plus-surrogate pipeline reaches mean percent errors of 0.73% for qubit frequency and 1.58% for anharmonicity, comparable to or below the fabrication and simulation-to-measurement uncertainty expected for academic-process transmon devices of this type. A single pipeline query takes approximately 56 ms on CPU, versus approximately 2 min for a conventional EM capacitance extraction on the same hardware, a speedup of more than 2,100 times. Batching minimizes the AI model inference overhead, reducing the runtime to 0.24 ms per sample on CPU and 2.5 microseconds per sample on GPU, resulting in speedups of 5.0 x 10^5 and 4.8 x 10^7, respectively, relative to a single conventional CPU EM extraction. Our results indicate that component-level inverse design usefully extends and complements conventional EM simulation, including for small datasets on the order of 1,000 samples.

title: An Operational Resolution Of The Third-Particle Paradox
authors: \v{c}aslav Brukner, Esteban Castro-Ruiz, Marius Krumm
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give an operational resolution of the third-particle paradox, relevant in the theory of quantum reference frames. The apparent paradox is that a system which is irrelevant in one quantum-reference-frame description can seem to become relevant after changing to another quantum reference frame, because the reduced state obtained after transforming a larger system need not agree with the state obtained by first discarding the extra system and then transforming. We argue that this comparison is not operationally meaningful unless the observables are transformed together with the states, or equivalently, unless the subsystem that needs to be discarded is properly identified. If the third particle is irrelevant for all measurements actually available in the original frame, then the transformed measurements form a restricted algebra in the new frame for which the third particle remains irrelevant. The paradox therefore results from replacing an operational statement about probabilities by a stronger, representation-dependent statement about equality of reduced density operators. We close by relating the question of when degrees of freedom may be discarded to the observable-induced, operational approach to subsystem structure.

result: They show that if the third particle is irrelevant for all measurements in the original frame, then after transformation the measurements form a restricted algebra where the particle remains irrelevant, resolving the paradox.
conclusion: The paradox arises from a representation-dependent comparison of reduced density operators rather than an operational statement about probabilities; the work emphasizes the need to transform observables alongside states.

title: Enabling Neutral Atom Integration: Redesigning Device Models For Universal Quantum Ecosystems
authors: Yannick Stade, Lukas Burgholzer, Ludwig Schmid, Robert Wille
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computing is transitioning from an academic idea to a practical technology, driven by recent hardware advancements and clear paths toward real-world applications. Universal quantum ecosystems (e.g., Qiskit, Cirq, PennyLane) facilitate this transition by providing a consistent interface to diverse quantum devices, abstracting hardware-specific details through a device model that captures each device's computational capabilities. However, these device models have historically been shaped by superconducting hardware, assuming static qubit positions and fixed coupling maps. This prevents them from representing the unique computational capabilities of emerging technologies such as neutral atoms, which feature dynamic qubit rearrangement and zoned operations. As a result, although numerous specialized compilers for neutral atom devices already exist, they cannot retrieve the hardware information they need through these ecosystems - creating a technology lock that hinders or even prevents the integration of neutral atom devices. In this work, we demonstrate how this limitation leads to suboptimal compilation results and can exclude certain devices entirely. Motivated by this, we propose rethinking current device models to faithfully represent neutral atom devices, enabling their seamless integration into universal quantum ecosystems. Evaluations conducted within the Quantum Device Management Interface (QDMI) demonstrate that the proposed device model unlocks a routing overhead fidelity improvement by a factor of up to 100,000 on a circuit with 16 qubits and 600 gates.

title: Conditional Probabilities In Quantum-optical Settings

title: Multicritical Dissipative Phase Transitions Manipulated By Dipole--dipole Interactions
authors: Jia-Xin Wang, Qian Bin, Jing-Jing Cao, Xin-You L\"{u}
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20905v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Precise control of criticality in superradiant phase transitions is essential for quantum state engineering and the simulation of nonequilibrium phase transitions. Here, we investigate theoretically multicritical phenomena in a dissipative two-Rydberg-atom cavity--QED system. The intrinisic dipole--dipole interaction between the two Rydberg atoms restructures the energy-level landscape of the atomic subsystem, thereby significantly modifying the boundary of the continuous second-order superradiant phase transition, and shifting both the phase boundary and the multicritical point toward weaker atom--cavity strengths. For sufficiently strong dipole--dipole interactions, the continuous second-order phase transition and the multicritical point both disappear, leaving only a discontinuous first--order phase transition that enables the emergence of a superradiant phase even at arbitrarily weak atom--cavity coupling. This work is of fundamental interest for studying dissipative quantum phase transitions, with potential implications for quantum precision measurement and quantum sensing.

title: Vacuum-induced Interference In Light Scattering By Multilevel Atomic Chains

abstract: ArXiv:2607.21073v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate cooperative light scattering by an ordered chain of multilevel atoms, which possess two quasi-resonant transitions with parallel dipole moments. Stage 3 applies this configuration to the reduced [MATH]-[MATH] ansatz, comparing ideal and noisy simulator-trained parameters. A supplementary noise analysis at [MATH] characterizes the depth-dependent interplay between circuit depth and DD effectiveness. The framework enables faithful QPE mimicry using a linearly scaling VQC, recovering the ground-state energy within the chemical accuracy threshold (1 kcal/mol), constituting a scalable, hardware-efficient paradigm for QPE-based molecular energy estimation on NISQ devices.
tldr: This paper presents a classical surrogate for quantum phase estimation using a shallow variational quantum circuit, applied to molecular energy estimation on NISQ hardware.
motivation: Quantum phase estimation requires deep circuits unsuitable for NISQ devices; the authors aim to create a hardware-efficient variational surrogate that avoids quantum simulation.
method: A variational quantum circuit is trained to reproduce the QPE measurement distribution using a classically computed Dirichlet kernel target, eliminating the exponential simulation bottleneck.
result: The framework recovers ground-state energy within chemical accuracy for H2 using a single-layer linear entangler ansatz on IBM Quantum hardware.
conclusion: The proposed surrogate enables scalable QPE-based molecular energy estimation on NISQ devices, but the contribution is primarily a computational technique without deep information-theoretic insights.

title: Monolithic Magneto-Optical Mach-Zehnder Isolator Using Laser-Annealed Iron Garnet On A Silicon Waveguide
authors: Tomoya Sugita, Reona Motoji, Yuki Yoshihara, Dan Maeda, Hiroki Yamamoto, Hibiki Miyashita, Kazushi Ishiyama, Taichi Goto
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stable silicon photonic circuits require monolithically integrated optical isolators based on magneto-optical garnet. However, crystallizing the garnet by conventional furnace annealing exposes the entire chip to high temperature and degrades the silicon waveguides and the metal electrodes. Here we avoid this degradation by using local laser annealing in vacuum to crystallize cerium-substituted yttrium iron garnet (Ce:YIG), deposited by ion beam sputtering without a seed layer, directly within a silicon-based Mach-Zehnder interferometer. A 915 nm beam heats only the garnet region confined in micrometer-scale trenches, leaving the surrounding circuit and electrodes intact. The device achieves an isolation ratio of 13.6 dB at a wavelength of 1540 nm, corresponding to a Faraday rotation of 0.092[MATH]/[MATH]m, with an insertion loss of 20.4 dB and a propagation loss of 9.5 dB. Transmission electron microscopy reveals the crystallized Ce:YIG and a ~10 nm boundary region at the interface with the Si waveguide. These results demonstrate that thermally sensitive silicon photonic devices and magneto-optical thin films requiring high-temperature processing can be integrated by a high-throughput technique compatible with mass production.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a monolithically integrated magneto-optical isolator on a silicon waveguide using laser-annealed Ce:YIG, achieving 13.6 dB isolation at 1540 nm.
motivation: Stable silicon photonic circuits require monolithically integrated optical isolators, but conventional furnace annealing degrades silicon waveguides and metal electrodes.
method: Local laser annealing in vacuum crystallizes Ce:YIG deposited by ion beam sputtering within micrometer-scale trenches on a silicon-based Mach-Zehnder interferometer.
result: The device achieves an isolation ratio of 13.6 dB at 1540 nm, with insertion loss 20.4 dB and propagation loss 9.5 dB; TEM reveals crystallized Ce:YIG with a ~10 nm boundary region.
conclusion: Thermally sensitive silicon photonic devices and magneto-optical thin films can be integrated via a high-throughput laser annealing technique compatible with mass production.

title: Entanglement, Evolutionary Stability, And Strategy-Space Dependence In An Ewl Quantum Game
authors: Derek Abbott Azhar Iqbal
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine how Eisert--Wilkens--Lewenstein (EWL) quantization affects evolutionary stability in a symmetric [MATH] game whose interior mixed Nash equilibrium is not evolutionarily stable. In the restricted two-parameter EWL strategy space, the quantum equilibrium [MATH] becomes a strict symmetric Nash equilibrium, and hence an evolutionarily stable strategy, for every [MATH]. Extending the admissible pure strategies to the full three-parameter [MATH] family preserves the Nash equilibrium but introduces a continuum of payoff-neutral mutants, causing strictness and the second ESS condition to fail. Thus, entanglement stabilizes the equilibrium only within the restricted EWL strategy space; the effect does not survive enlargement to full [MATH].
tldr: This paper studies evolutionary stability in quantum games using EWL quantization, finding that entanglement stabilizes equilibria only in a restricted strategy space.
motivation: To understand how quantum entanglement affects evolutionary stability in game theory, specifically in the context of the EWL quantization scheme.
method: The authors analyze a symmetric 2x2 game with an interior mixed Nash equilibrium that is not evolutionarily stable, and apply EWL quantization to study the stability of the quantum equilibrium under restricted and full strategy spaces.
result: In the restricted two-parameter EWL strategy space, the quantum equilibrium becomes a strict symmetric Nash equilibrium and evolutionarily stable for all entanglement values. However, extending to the full three-parameter family preserves the Nash equilibrium but introduces payoff-neutral mutants, causing strictness and the second ESS condition to fail.
conclusion: Entanglement stabilizes the equilibrium only within the restricted EWL strategy space; the effect does not survive enlargement to the full strategy space.

title: Kaplansky's Second Test Problem In Operator Algebras
authors: Chunlan Jiang, Minghui Ma, Rui Shi, Yuanhang Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kaplansky's second test problem on similarity asks: if [MATH] and [MATH] are elements in a unital Banach algebra [MATH] and [MATH] is similar to [MATH] in [MATH], is [MATH] similar to [MATH] in [MATH]? We answer this problem affirmatively if [MATH] is an operator with property [MATH] in a type [MATH] von Neumann algebra [MATH], i.e., [MATH] contains a bounded maximal abelian family of idempotents. Moreover, the condition of property [MATH] can be removed for [MATH]. A similar result is proved if [MATH] is an element in a unital Banach algebra [MATH] with essentially finite-dimensional commutant, i.e., the relative commutant of [MATH] in [MATH] is finite-dimensional modulo its Jacobson radical. Finally, we point out that one of our main results can be applied to the implementation of local unitary (LU) equivalence of quantum states.
tldr: This paper solves Kaplansky's second test problem on similarity for operators with property (P) in type I von Neumann algebras, with an application to local unitary equivalence of quantum states.
motivation: Kaplansky's test problems are fundamental in operator algebras; solving them has implications for the structure of von Neumann algebras and their applications.
method: The authors use operator-theoretic techniques, including the concept of property (P) and analysis of commutants modulo Jacobson radical, to prove similarity results.
result: They affirmatively answer Kaplansky's second test problem for operators with property (P) in type I von Neumann algebras, and also for elements with essentially finite-dimensional commutant in unital Banach algebras.
conclusion: The results provide new insights into similarity in operator algebras and can be applied to local unitary equivalence of quantum states, linking operator theory to quantum information.

title: Machine-Learned Compact Subspace Generation For Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction Within Density Matrix Embedding Framework
authors: Ashish Kumar Patra, Anurag K. S. V., Ruchika Bhat, Sai Shankar P., Rahul Maitra, Jaiganesh G
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20585v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD), an extension of Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction (QSCI), has emerged as a promising hybrid quantum-classical paradigm for computing molecular ground state energies. By leveraging quantum sampling instead of variational optimization, QSCI avoids barren plateaus and enables direct reconstruction of correlated electronic wavefunctions. However, existing configuration recovery techniques primarily enforce symmetry constraints without guaranteeing optimal selection of the most physically relevant configurations, often leading to unnecessarily large subspaces and increased classical diagonalization costs. In this work, we introduce a machine-learned compact subspace generation protocol based on Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), termed QSCI-RBM, and integrate it within the Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET) framework. The RBM is trained on quantum-sampled configurations to learn the underlying probability distribution of dominant determinants, enabling the targeted generation of high-probability configurations. We apply this framework to the simulation of a protein-ligand complex involving the inhibitor Carmofur bound to the SARS-CoV-2 main protease ([MATH]). Our results demonstrate that DMET-QSCI-RBM achieves energies within the chemical accuracy threshold by accessing only approximately 4% of the configuration subspace. In contrast, standard DMET-SQD simulations failed to reach chemical accuracy while accessing up to 20% of the subspace, even as the chemical potential itself nearly converged. These findings highlight that RBM-assisted configuration generation produces significantly more compact subspaces while preserving physical accuracy, thereby reducing classical computational overhead and enabling the scalable quantum embedding simulation of complex biological systems.
tldr: This paper combines machine learning (RBM) with quantum selected configuration interaction and density matrix embedding to compute molecular ground state energies, focusing on quantum chemistry rather than quantum information theory.
motivation: Existing configuration recovery techniques in quantum-classical hybrid methods often produce unnecessarily large subspaces, increasing classical diagonalization costs. The authors aim to generate more compact subspaces while preserving accuracy.
method: A Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) is trained on quantum-sampled configurations to learn the probability distribution of dominant determinants, enabling targeted generation of high-probability configurations within the Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET) framework.
result: The DMET-QSCI-RBM method achieves chemical accuracy using only about 4% of the configuration subspace, whereas standard DMET-SQD fails to reach chemical accuracy even with 20% of the subspace.
conclusion: RBM-assisted configuration generation produces significantly more compact subspaces while maintaining physical accuracy, reducing classical overhead and enabling scalable quantum embedding simulations of complex biological systems.

title: Detecting Hidden Nonlinear High Frequency Modes Beyond Fundamental Minimal Temporal Resolution Using Weak Measurements
authors: Igor Prlina
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work we study whether nonlinear models of quantum mechanics can avoid detection by strong measurements, if the nonlinear effects only exist as high frequency modes. A potential physical process which could hide such modes would be amplitude level time averaging over fundamentally indistinguishable times. To that end, we have defined a temporal indistinguishability postulate which describes the averaging process, and handcrafted a nonlinear toy model well suited to avoid detection. We have demonstrated that even in such an ideal setup, tabletop weak postselected measurements can still detect nonlinear behavior and put constraints on nonlinear high frequency modes of evolution, even at frequencies beyond fundamental minimal temporal resolution.
tldr: The paper proposes a nonlinear quantum toy model with high-frequency modes that evade strong measurements but can be detected via weak measurements.
motivation: To explore whether nonlinear quantum effects could be hidden from standard measurements due to temporal averaging, and to test if weak measurements can reveal them.
method: Defines a temporal indistinguishability postulate and constructs a nonlinear toy model; uses weak postselected measurements to detect nonlinear behavior.
result: Weak measurements can detect nonlinear high-frequency modes even beyond the fundamental minimal temporal resolution.
conclusion: Nonlinear quantum effects, if they exist, may be detectable via weak measurements despite being hidden from strong measurements.

title: Affine Extension Of The Free-Particle--Oscillator--Inverted-Oscillator Triangle
authors: Mikhail S. Plyushchay Andrey Alcala
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the one-dimensional linear-potential system as an affine extension of the conformal triangle formed by the free particle, harmonic oscillator (HO) and inverted harmonic oscillator (IHO). Unlike these homogeneous quadratic Hamiltonians in the [MATH] sector, the linear-potential Hamiltonian involves the Heisenberg ideal of the Schr\"odinger algebra. Its direct relation to the free particle is a regular accelerated-frame transformation, developed here at the levels of the classical action, canonical transformation, wave-function intertwiner and propagator; its HO and IHO realizations instead arise through singular displaced-oscillator limits. The Airy energy eigenstates follow from a cubic-phase transform of free-particle momentum eigenstates, from condensation of highly excited harmonic-oscillator levels, and from the limit of a subdominant parabolic-cylinder scattering branch of the inverted oscillator. We also develop a planar extension in homogeneous crossed electric and magnetic fields, where uniform acceleration generates the electric interaction, while uniform rotation produces the Landau coupling and the centrifugal inverted-oscillator term; the guiding-center dynamics yields the Hall drift.
tldr: This paper studies the affine extension of the free-particle–oscillator–inverted-oscillator triangle, focusing on the linear-potential system and its connections via transformations and limits.
motivation: To understand the algebraic and dynamical relationships between the free particle, harmonic oscillator, and inverted oscillator through an affine extension of the conformal triangle.
method: The authors develop regular and singular transformations at the levels of classical action, canonical transformation, wave-function intertwiner, and propagator, and also consider a planar extension in crossed electric and magnetic fields.
result: The linear-potential system is shown to be an affine extension, with Airy eigenstates derived from free-particle momentum eigenstates via a cubic-phase transform, condensation of highly excited oscillator levels, and a limit of the inverted oscillator's scattering branch.
conclusion: The work provides a unified framework connecting these fundamental quantum systems, but does not directly address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Emergent Non-Equilibrium Emission Profiles Via Luminescent Angle Restriction For Photovoltaic Energy Conversion
authors: Jonathan Mctague (department Of Chemistry, University Of California, Irvine), Rivi Ratnaweera (department Of Chemistry, Texas A&M University), Matthew Sheldon
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20783v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The detailed-balance method established by Shockley and Queisser determines photovoltaic (PV) conversion efficiencies by relating non-equilibrium converter operation to an equilibrium reference state. Conventionally, the angular and spectral radiative channels during power conversion are assumed to be defined by the equilibrium absorptivity and emissivity, with the photon chemical potential setting their occupation. This assumption is well motivated for flat-plate cells, but requires closer examination when radiative energy is redistributed within a more complex nanophotonic architecture. We analyze this distinction with a proposed luminescent angle restrictor (LAR), in which a flat-plate PV absorber is coupled to an overlayer with vertically aligned nanorods (NR). The NR layer is nearly transparent to near-normal sunlight, while oblique PV luminescence can be absorbed, re-emitted, and partially returned to the absorber. To calculate the operating emission profile, we develop an ergodic Markov chain transport model enforcing microscopic reversibility for local optical transitions without imposing a fixed macroscopic emissivity. The model recovers the flat-plate detailed-balance limit and predicts voltage-dependent external emission profiles from the LAR/PV architecture. Under idealized conditions, this non-equilibrium angular redistribution reduces the angular entropy of luminescent emission and increases efficiency relative to the conventional flat-plate reference. We also evaluate NR photoluminescence quantum yield, solar misalignment, orientational disorder, and Auger recombination to identify practical constraints on the proposed architecture. These results show how detailed-balance limits for PV structures can depend on internal radiative energy redistribution and the non-equilibrium emission profile, beyond what can be inferred from the macroscopic equilibrium optical response.
tldr: This paper studies non-equilibrium emission profiles in photovoltaic devices using a luminescent angle restrictor, focusing on efficiency improvements via angular redistribution of luminescent light.
motivation: To understand how detailed-balance limits for photovoltaic conversion depend on internal radiative energy redistribution beyond equilibrium assumptions.
method: Develops an ergodic Markov chain transport model that enforces microscopic reversibility for local optical transitions without imposing fixed macroscopic emissivity.
result: The model recovers the flat-plate detailed-balance limit and predicts voltage-dependent external emission profiles; under idealized conditions, angular redistribution reduces angular entropy and increases efficiency.
conclusion: Detailed-balance limits for photovoltaic structures can depend on non-equilibrium emission profiles, beyond what equilibrium optical response predicts.

title: Measurement Of The Reduced Dipole Matrix Element In Ba$^+$
authors: N. Jayjong, M. D. K. Lee, K. J. Arnold, M. D. Barrett
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a high-precision measurement of the reduced electric-dipole matrix element [MATH] in [MATH]. By comparing off-resonant scattering rates with dispersive Stark-shift measurements, we determine the matrix element to be [MATH], corresponding to a [MATH] excited-state radiative lifetime of [MATH]~ns. Combining our experimental results with a prior model for the differential scalar polarizability [MATH], we extract the static value [MATH]a.u. This determination directly improves the evaluation of the blackbody radiation (BBR) shift, minimizing a prominent systematic limitation in room-temperature [MATH] optical clock error budgets. motivation: Accurate knowledge of the dipole matrix element is needed to reduce systematic uncertainties in Ba+ optical clocks, particularly the blackbody radiation shift.
method: Off-resonant scattering rates are compared with dispersive Stark-shift measurements to determine the matrix element, and combined with a prior polarizability model.
result: The reduced dipole matrix element is measured with high precision, yielding a radiative lifetime of ~6.3 ns and a static differential polarizability of 36.2 a.u.
conclusion: The measurement improves BBR shift evaluation and provides a benchmark for atomic-structure calculations, benefiting quantum metrology and fundamental physics tests.

title: Generation Of Bright Quantum High-order Harmonic Driven By Combined Coherent And Bright Squeezed Vacuum Light
authors: Wentao Wang, Yaoshun Sun, Liyuan Wang, Lingrui Hu, Dajun Ding, Xiangyu Tang, Mingxuan Li, Jianmin Yuan, Sizuo Luo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attosecond quantum light, formed by the superposition of high-order harmonics driven by intense quantum light, opens new routes to probe quantum-mechanical correlations in matter. In this study, we have investigated the macroscopic propagation effects of quantum high-order harmonics generated by the combination of strong coherent and weak bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) lasers interacting with atomic gas. Our results reveal that the pressure-dependent intensity of harmonics arising from absorbing or emitting BSV photons differs from that of harmonics generated using only strong coherent pulses. Macroscopic propagation simulations indicate that the action phase of harmonics is perturbed by the weak BSV pulses. This perturbation modulates the phase mismatch of sub-cycle attosecond bursts and affects their quantum properties when the gas pressure varies. The ability to generate bright quantum high-order harmonics lays a foundation for the establishment and application of attosecond quantum spectroscopy.
tldr: This paper studies macroscopic propagation effects of quantum high-order harmonics generated by combining coherent and bright squeezed vacuum light, focusing on attosecond quantum spectroscopy.
motivation: To understand how weak bright squeezed vacuum pulses affect the phase matching and quantum properties of high-order harmonics, enabling bright quantum harmonic generation for attosecond quantum spectroscopy.
method: The authors perform macroscopic propagation simulations of high-order harmonic generation driven by a combination of strong coherent and weak bright squeezed vacuum lasers interacting with atomic gas, analyzing pressure-dependent intensity and phase mismatch.
result: The pressure-dependent harmonic intensity differs when absorbing or emitting squeezed vacuum photons, and the weak BSV pulses perturb the action phase, modulating phase mismatch of sub-cycle attosecond bursts.
conclusion: Bright quantum high-order harmonics can be generated, laying a foundation for attosecond quantum spectroscopy.

title: Topological Measures In Weighted Hypergraphs
authors: Ekaterina Vasilyeva, Liubov Tupikina, Daniil Musatov, Andrei M. Raigorodskii, Charo. I. Del Genio, Stefano Boccaletti
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Higher-order interactions introduce an additional structural dimension to complex networks, requiring consistent generalizations of classical topological measures. In hypergraphs, the definition of distance between nodes is not unique: beyond the conventional measure derived from clique projection, an alternative formulation that explicitly incorporates the sizes of hyperedges, those of their intersection and their weights has been recently proposed. Here, we generalize three distance-based topological measures, namely closeness centrality, betweenness centrality and node eccentricity, using this new hypergraph distance. Trough tractable illustrative examples, we demonstrate that the differences between results obtained with the two distances are systematic and arise from structurally meaningful features of the higher-order networks. Also, analyzing a series of real-world datasets, we show that hypergraphs can be divided into three distinct classes, corresponding to the possible dominance of specific orders of interaction over their general metric structure. This provides practical guidance on the possibility of limiting the analysis to only some specific interaction orders, reducing its complexity while maintaining the full information of the system.
tldr: This paper generalizes distance-based topological measures to weighted hypergraphs, focusing on higher-order interactions in complex networks.
motivation: Standard network measures rely on pairwise distances, but hypergraphs require generalizations that account for hyperedge sizes and weights to capture higher-order interactions.
method: The authors generalize closeness centrality, betweenness centrality, and node eccentricity using a recently proposed hypergraph distance that incorporates hyperedge sizes, intersections, and weights.
result: Systematic differences between the new measures and those based on clique projection are demonstrated on illustrative examples, and real-world datasets reveal three classes of hypergraphs based on dominant interaction orders.
conclusion: The work provides practical guidance for analyzing hypergraphs by focusing on specific interaction orders, reducing complexity while preserving information.

title: Statistical Analysis Of Speckle Fields
authors: Ian D. Min-Roberts, Wojciech Rozmus, Pierre A. Michel
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speckles, or laser hot spots, are the intensity maxima of optically smoothed laser beams that seed instabilities, making a quantitative statistical description of speckles of interest. Earlier statistical theories estimated the number of speckles above an intensity level set for optically smoothed beams produced by random phase plates, using an ansatz that relates intensity maxima to the maxima of the real and imaginary components of the underlying complex Gaussian electric field. Here, we count speckles directly from the laser intensity field, treating it as a [MATH] random field and imposing the local maximum conditions without a single-component ansatz. We evaluate the theory for square, circular, annular, and Gaussian aperture spectra, and include induced spatial incoherence as a temporal smoothing mechanism. Monte Carlo simulations confirm the theory and show improved accuracy relative to the earlier ansatz-based formulation. Applications include a simple SBS reflectivity model using the resulting speckle statistics, and a comparison between speckle-driven and thermal noise density-fluctuation spectra.
tldr: This paper develops a statistical theory for counting speckles in laser intensity fields, validated by Monte Carlo simulations.
motivation: Speckles in laser beams seed instabilities, so a quantitative statistical description is needed for applications like inertial confinement fusion.
method: Treats the intensity field as a χ² random field and imposes local maximum conditions directly, without the earlier single-component ansatz.
result: The new theory shows improved accuracy over the ansatz-based formulation for various aperture spectra, confirmed by simulations.
conclusion: The speckle statistics can be applied to model SBS reflectivity and compare speckle-driven vs. thermal noise density fluctuations.

title: Polarization Vector Conjugation In A Photonic Integrated Circuit
authors: Anna J. Miller, Carson G. Valdez, Anne R. Kroo, Marko \v{s}imi\'c, Marek Vlk, Charles Roques-Carmes, David A. B. Miller, Olav Solgaard
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show how to perform polarization conjugation of light in a simple apparatus without any nonlinear optical materials, based on self-configuring Mach-Zehnder interferometers fed by a polarization splitter. This allows us to completely and automatically remove the polarization variations on a single beam or mode propagating through an optical system with arbitrary birefringence, such as a conventional optical fiber, and compensate polarization variations experienced in the forward direction by propagating the conjugated beam back through the system and recreating the original polarization at the source. We demonstrate this polarization conjugation in an optical fiber setup in different orientations with a measured polarization extinction ratio of -30 dB for the returned beam.
tldr: This paper demonstrates polarization conjugation in a photonic integrated circuit using self-configuring Mach-Zehnder interferometers, enabling automatic compensation of polarization variations in optical fibers.
motivation: Polarization variations in optical fibers degrade signal quality; a method to automatically conjugate and compensate polarization without nonlinear materials is needed.
method: The authors use a polarization splitter followed by self-configuring Mach-Zehnder interferometers to perform polarization conjugation, then propagate the conjugated beam back through the system.
result: They achieve a polarization extinction ratio of -30 dB for the returned beam in an optical fiber setup, demonstrating effective compensation.
conclusion: Polarization conjugation can be performed in a simple, all-linear photonic circuit, offering a practical solution for polarization compensation in fiber-optic systems.

title: An Operator-Algebraic Exposition Of The Thirring-Wehrl Theory Of The Quasi-Spin Bcs Model
authors: Yoshitsugu Sekine
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This expository review reformulates the BCS analyses of Haag, Emch--Guenin, and Thirring--Wehrl, together with subsequent operator-algebraic mean-field results of B\'ona, Raggio--Werner, and Bru--de Siqueira Pedra, in the language of quasi-local [MATH]-algebras and state decompositions. The quasi-spin model is realized on the UHF algebra of type [MATH], with product sectors described by von Neumann's incomplete infinite tensor products. This framework distinguishes strong limits of intensive observables, domain-restricted limits of extensive observables, and sectorwise Bogoliubov--Haag limits, including their operator criterion, gap equation, and limiting dynamics. In the degenerate model, the ground-state and thermal gauge averages admit central direct-integral decompositions over the gauge circle, and the thermal decomposition converges to the ground-state decomposition at zero temperature. Adjoining the gauge phase as a central classical variable combines the phase-dependent Bogoliubov dynamics into one automorphism group on [MATH].
tldr: This paper provides an operator-algebraic reformulation of the BCS quasi-spin model, focusing on mathematical structures like UHF algebras and state decompositions.
motivation: To present a unified operator-algebraic exposition of the Thirring-Wehrl theory of the quasi-spin BCS model, clarifying the mathematical foundations.
method: The paper uses quasi-local C*-algebras, von Neumann infinite tensor products, and central direct-integral decompositions to analyze the model's thermodynamics and dynamics.
result: It distinguishes various limits of observables, derives the gap equation, and shows convergence of thermal to ground-state decompositions at zero temperature.
conclusion: The operator-algebraic framework provides a rigorous mathematical description of the BCS model's equilibrium states and dynamics.

title: Hierarchical Log-Gaussian Relaxation On A Fixed D3q125 Velocity Set
authors: Bj{\o}rn Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a hierarchical order-resolved relaxation model for a fixed D3Q125 discrete-velocity kinetic formulation. Conventional adaptive collision models often use one scalar rarefaction or nonequilibrium indicator for all retained moment orders, thereby coupling distinct kinetic sectors. Here, a shared macroscopic-gradient background is combined separately with second-, third-, and fourth-order thermodynamic nonequilibrium indicators to define effective measures K2, K3, and K4, each driving its own log-Gaussian relaxation spectrum. Pure-order perturbation tests verify selective activation, with nonmatching sectors remaining at roundoff level. Homogeneous mixed-order, amplitude, and composition tests show lower residual nonequilibrium than a common-sensor model while preserving positive populations. In a smooth periodic compression wave at the stated reference discretization and in the TNE-only sensor limit, the peak total nonequilibrium intensity is reduced by 6.565%, with reductions throughout the domain and in all retained moment sectors. Additional timestep, transport-discretization, relaxation-spectrum, uniform-boost, long-time, and shear-wave studies show that the sign of the hierarchical correction is robust over the tested configurations, while its magnitude depends on timestep, transport scheme, sensor frame, and relaxation spectrum. The periodic benchmarks preserve the principal global invariants to floating-point accuracy and remain positive. These results establish the mechanism and numerical behavior of order-resolved activation on a fixed velocity set; independent kinetic-reference validation is still required before claiming universal accuracy improvement.
tldr: This paper develops a hierarchical order-resolved relaxation model for a fixed D3Q125 discrete-velocity kinetic formulation, using log-Gaussian relaxation spectra driven by thermodynamic nonequilibrium indicators.
motivation: Conventional adaptive collision models use a single scalar rarefaction indicator for all moment orders, coupling distinct kinetic sectors. The authors aim to decouple these sectors by introducing order-specific relaxation.
method: A shared macroscopic-gradient background is combined separately with second-, third-, and fourth-order thermodynamic nonequilibrium indicators to define effective measures K2, K3, and K4, each driving its own log-Gaussian relaxation spectrum. Pure-order perturbation tests and various numerical experiments are performed.
result: The hierarchical model shows selective activation of targeted moment orders, lower residual nonequilibrium than a common-sensor model, and a 6.565% reduction in peak total nonequilibrium intensity in a smooth periodic compression wave, while preserving positivity and global invariants.
conclusion: The mechanism and numerical behavior of order-resolved activation on a fixed velocity set are established, but independent kinetic-reference validation is still required before claiming universal accuracy improvement.

title: Weak Private Information Retrieval For Graph-based Storage
authors: Shodasakshari Vidya, Chandan Anand, Prasad Krishnan
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A distributed storage system with graph-based replication consists of a collection of databases and the files they contain. The databases (or servers) are represented as the vertices of a graph, while each file is stored in a distinct pair of servers and is represented by an edge of this graph. Private information retrieval (G-PIR) on such a graph-based storage system involves a client which seeks to retrieve a desired file via a query-response protocol, without leaking the identity of the desired file index to any database. The goal of G-PIR is to maximize the rate (reciprocal of the total normalized download) under the privacy constraint. Prior work on G-PIR has involved perfect information-theoretic privacy (i.e., null leakage). However, if the privacy constraint is relaxed, then PIR protocols could be designed that have even higher rates. We term such protocols as Graph-based Weak Private Information Retrieval (G-WPIR) protocols and initiate their formal study in this work. We propose a G-WPIR scheme for arbitrary graphs, and identify the trade-offs it achieves between rate and privacy, under two well known leakage metrics: mutual information leakage and maximal leakage. Our protocol employs minimal subpacketization (representing a file-size constraint) and employs a simple probabilistic query realization to obtain the smooth trade-off. We extend this protocol with some modifications to two special classes of graphs, the complete graphs and the complete bipartite graphs, and identify the corresponding rate-privacy trade-offs achieved.
tldr: This paper studies weak private information retrieval on graph-based distributed storage systems, focusing on rate-privacy trade-offs under relaxed privacy constraints.
motivation: Prior work on graph-based PIR assumed perfect privacy, but relaxing privacy can yield higher rates. The authors initiate the formal study of weak PIR for graph-based storage.
method: They propose a G-WPIR scheme for arbitrary graphs using minimal subpacketization and probabilistic query realization, and extend it to complete and complete bipartite graphs.
result: The scheme achieves smooth rate-privacy trade-offs under mutual information and maximal leakage metrics, with explicit trade-off expressions for special graph classes.
conclusion: Weak PIR can significantly improve rates over perfect PIR at the cost of some privacy leakage, and the proposed scheme provides a flexible trade-off.

title: Equivalence Of Sofic $p$-Metric Mean Dimensions And A Tame-Metric Variational Formula
authors: Zhuowei Liu Xianqiang Li
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21376v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a countable discrete sofic group acting by homeomorphisms on a compact metrizable space [MATH] and [MATH] a sofic approximation of [MATH]. We prove that for every [MATH], the sofic [MATH]-metric mean dimension is equivalent to the sofic metric mean dimension, i.e there exists a common value [MATH] such that, $[MATH][MATH]1\leq q\leq\infty[MATH][MATH][MATH]\mathcal T(X)[MATH]X$ having tame growth of covering numbers.

motivation: To unify different definitions of metric mean dimension for sofic group actions and extend variational principles to systems with tame growth of covering numbers.
method: Uses sofic approximations and topological dynamics to compare p-metric mean dimensions and derive a variational formula.

conclusion: The results provide a unified framework for metric mean dimension in sofic group actions, with applications to systems having tame covering number growth.

title: Improved Lower Bounds For The Shannon Capacity Of Odd Cycles
authors: Nathaniel Itty, Christopher D. Rosin, Chase Carstensen, Daniel Reichman

It is lower bounded by [MATH] for any [MATH], where [MATH] is the independence number of the [MATH]-th strong power of [MATH]. We construct independent sets of size [MATH] in [MATH], [MATH] in [MATH], and [MATH] in [MATH], improving the best known lower bounds for the Shannon capacity of these graphs to [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH]. title: Construction And Dynamic Update Of Channel Gain Maps Via 3d Gaussian Splatting
authors: Yilong Chen, Yuan Guo, Juncong Zhou, Jie Xu, Rui Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21099v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Channel knowledge maps (CKMs) have emerged as a promising technique for providing scene-specific and location-dependent propagation knowledge to enable environment-aware wireless network design. This paper investigates the construction and dynamic updating of a particular type of CKM, namely grid-based channel gain maps (CGMs), for large-scale networks using three-dimensional Gaussian splatting (3DGS). First, we formulate a grid-based channel gain model, where each map entry is defined as the locally averaged channel gain over a receiver grid, thereby suppressing phase-sensitive small-scale fluctuations. The resulting channel gain is decomposed into distance-dependent attenuation, path transmittance, and effective scattering contributions. Based on this decomposition, we develop a physics-informed Gaussian-splatting-based channel gain (GS-CG) model, which represents the propagation environment as a set of Gaussian primitives. The proposed model maps Gaussian geometry, opacity, and directional features to propagation-related factors and renders grid-level channel gains through a differentiable process. To accommodate real-time environmental changes, we further propose an incremental learning mechanism that updates a static reference GS-CG representation into a dynamic CGM. Specifically, the reference Gaussian primitives are frozen, while a compact set of tunable Gaussians is introduced to capture newly induced local channel-gain variations from sparse measurements.Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed GS-CG methods accurately reconstruct grid-based CGMs, efficiently adapt to dynamic environmental changes, and achieve a favorable accuracy-complexity tradeoff for fast CGM refinement.
tldr: This paper uses 3D Gaussian splatting to construct and dynamically update channel gain maps for wireless communication networks.
motivation: Channel knowledge maps (CKMs) are needed for environment-aware wireless network design, but existing methods lack efficient dynamic updating for large-scale networks.
method: A physics-informed Gaussian-splatting-based channel gain (GS-CG) model is proposed, representing the propagation environment as Gaussian primitives and rendering grid-level channel gains via differentiable rendering; an incremental learning mechanism updates the model with sparse measurements.
result: The proposed GS-CG methods accurately reconstruct grid-based channel gain maps and efficiently adapt to dynamic environmental changes with favorable accuracy-complexity tradeoff.
conclusion: 3D Gaussian splatting is effective for constructing and updating channel gain maps, enabling fast CGM refinement for wireless networks.

title: Exact Ensemble Controllability For Neural Differential Equations Via Neural Interpolation
authors: Martin Gugat
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a system that is governed by neural dynamics. Neural dynamics are a model for deep neural networks with a large number of layers. For a differential equation where the right-hand side is given by a neural network, we analyze the exact ensemble controllability of the system. This property plays an essential role in Machine Learning. It concerns the ability to learn to perform different tasks simultaneously with a single neural dynamics: Exact ensemble controllability requires that [MATH] different initial states are steered to corresponding [MATH] target states with a single set of control parameters. We present a constructive solution to the problem. The construction is based on the solution of a neural interpolation problem. We show that if the right-hand side of the differential equation is given by a neural network of depth two, the interpolation problem can be reduced to the solution of a system of linear equations.
tldr: This paper studies exact ensemble controllability for neural differential equations using neural interpolation, which is a topic in machine learning and control theory, not quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The ability to steer multiple initial states to target states with a single set of control parameters is essential for multi-task learning in deep neural networks.
method: The paper reduces the controllability problem to a neural interpolation problem and shows that for a depth-two neural network, the interpolation reduces to solving a linear system.
result: A constructive solution for exact ensemble controllability is provided, demonstrating that a single neural dynamics can simultaneously perform multiple tasks.
conclusion: The work contributes to the theoretical foundations of neural network training but does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: A Log-majorization Inequality For Normal Matrices With Applications To Determinantal Inequalities And Geometric Means
authors: Mohammad Mahdi Ghabries
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a log-majorization inequality comparing the eigenvalues of the interlaced product [MATH] with those of [MATH], valid for every positive semi-definite [MATH] and every normal [MATH], with the inequality reversing for [MATH] when [MATH] is positive definite. This extends known Hermitian results to the strictly larger class of normal matrices, where normality is shown to be the exact structural hypothesis, not a technical convenience. A counterexample proves the result can fail without it. As applications, we settle a normal-matrix extension of a determinantal conjecture of Lin, proving $[MATH][MATH]A[MATH]B[MATH]p \ge 0$, and we give a complete eigenvalue picture for products of weighted geometric means, sharpening and complementing a theorem of Hiai and Lin.
tldr: This paper proves a log-majorization inequality for normal matrices and applies it to determinantal inequalities and geometric means.
motivation: Extend known Hermitian matrix inequalities to the larger class of normal matrices, settling a conjecture of Lin.
method: Uses matrix analysis and majorization theory, with counterexamples to show necessity of normality.
result: Establishes the log-majorization inequality and proves a normal-matrix extension of Lin's determinantal conjecture.
conclusion: Normality is the exact structural hypothesis for the inequality, and the results sharpen prior work on geometric means.

title: A Kuramoto Phase Model To Explore The Synchronisation Of A Network Of Circadian Clocks
authors: Franck Delaunay (IBV), Antoine Fortun\'e (IBV), Ines Krawczyk (IBV), Mar\'echal Anastasia (maiage), Mathieu Mezache (maiage, MUSCA), Laurent Tournier
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21214v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a model of the circadian clock in a population of cells based on a network of oscillators, derived from the Kuramoto model. The coupling between oscillators is described by a global interaction term but we introduce a phase-dependent coupling mechanism, such that oscillators interact only within a specific interval of the cycle corresponding to a specific stage of the circadian cycle. We analytically demonstrate that this modified system achieves complete asymptotic phase synchronisation, provided specific conditions on the initial phase distribution and the coupling window length are met. To bridge this theoretical framework with experimental observations, we introduce a signal processing procedure based on wavelet decomposition to extract quantitative oscillatory features from Per2::luciferase reporter traces. We then calibrate the model against datasets from both wild type and Cry2 knockout hepatocyte spheroids using a two-step quasi-Monte Carlo filtering algorithm. The comparative analysis reveals significant phenotypic divergence, showing that the Cry2KO condition alters the identifiability landscape of the model's parameters and introduces new compensatory mechanisms that confound the initial population heterogeneity with long-term macroscopic signal decay.
tldr: This paper models circadian clock synchronization in cell populations using a modified Kuramoto model with phase-dependent coupling, calibrated against experimental data.
motivation: Understanding synchronization of circadian clocks in cell populations is important for chronobiology, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: A Kuramoto model with phase-dependent coupling is analyzed analytically for synchronization conditions, and a wavelet-based signal processing procedure is used to calibrate the model against Per2::luciferase reporter data from wild-type and Cry2 knockout hepatocyte spheroids.
result: Complete asymptotic phase synchronization is achieved under specific conditions; Cry2 knockout alters parameter identifiability and introduces compensatory mechanisms.
conclusion: The model captures phenotypic differences in circadian rhythms, but the work is purely classical and biological, with no quantum or information-theoretic content.

title: 3d Uncertainty Quantification For The Photo-Acoustic Tomography
authors: Babak Maboudi Afkham, Amal Mohammed A Alghami, Hassan Yazdanian, Tanja Tarvainen
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photoacoustic tomography (PAT) is a promising modality for high-resolution biomedical imaging, motivating the need for reliable uncertainty quantification (UQ) of reconstructed images. Bayesian approaches provide a rigorous framework for UQ but remain computationally challenging for realistic three-dimensional PAT and are sensitive to numerical approximations in the governing wave equation. We develop a finite-element Bayesian UQ framework for PAT that accommodates complex computational domains and detector geometries while enabling large-scale three-dimensional inference. The proposed methodology reformulates the randomize-then-optimize (RTO) sampling strategy as a matrix-free algorithm that generates independent posterior samples using only forward and adjoint wave propagations. Particular attention is given to constructing an adjoint discretization that forms an exact transpose pair with the discrete forward operator while remaining consistent with the continuous PAT adjoint, enabling efficient least-squares solvers within the sampling procedure. We investigate the influence of temporal discretization, artificial boundary conditions, and adjoint consistency on posterior uncertainty and identify discretization strategies that avoid numerical artifacts. The framework is validated against exact posterior statistics, existing Bayesian PAT methods, and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo using the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), and is demonstrated on a three-dimensional problem with approximately [MATH] unknowns on a general finite-element domain. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first large-scale Bayesian PAT study on general three-dimensional finite-element geometries, and the methodology extends naturally to a broad class of linear PDE-constrained inverse problems.
tldr: This paper develops a Bayesian uncertainty quantification framework for photoacoustic tomography, a biomedical imaging modality.
motivation: Photoacoustic tomography requires reliable uncertainty quantification for reconstructed images, but existing methods are computationally challenging for 3D problems and sensitive to numerical approximations.
method: The authors propose a matrix-free randomize-then-optimize (RTO) sampling strategy combined with finite-element discretization, ensuring adjoint consistency for efficient least-squares solvers.
result: The framework is validated against exact posterior statistics and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, and demonstrated on a 3D problem with approximately 10^6 unknowns on a general finite-element domain.
conclusion: This is the first large-scale Bayesian PAT study on general 3D finite-element geometries, and the methodology extends to a broad class of linear PDE-constrained inverse problems.

title: Gpe: Evaluating Robust Evidence Aggregation For Fact Verification Under Controllable GEO-Style Poisoning
authors: Zhaoqi Wang, Zijian Zhang, Xiaomei Yuan, Pengtao Kou, Jiamou Liu, Zhen Li, Liehuang Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20730v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models increasingly use search tools to retrieve up-to-date information, introducing a new attack surface in which retrieved documents can be manipulated. This risk is amplified by the development of generative engine optimization, which can make selected content more likely to be retrieved, cited, and adopted by models. Existing fact-verification benchmarks and evaluation frameworks do not provide the controlled evidence environments needed to assess robustness against GEO poisoning. We therefore propose GPE, which consists of a multi-domain fact-verification benchmark and an evaluation framework for controlling evidence sources and poisoning ratios. Experiments across multiple verification methods and poisoning attacks demonstrate that GPE exposes robustness degradation and efficiency trade-offs that cannot be observed through clean evaluation alone, confirming the need to evaluate fact verification under adversarial evidence environments.
tldr: This paper proposes a benchmark and evaluation framework for assessing fact verification robustness against generative engine optimization poisoning.
motivation: Large language models using search tools are vulnerable to manipulated retrieved documents, but existing benchmarks lack controlled environments to evaluate robustness against such poisoning.
method: The authors introduce GPE, a multi-domain fact-verification benchmark with an evaluation framework that controls evidence sources and poisoning ratios, and test various verification methods under different poisoning attacks.
result: Experiments show that GPE reveals robustness degradation and efficiency trade-offs not observable in clean evaluation, confirming the need for adversarial evaluation.
conclusion: Fact verification systems must be evaluated under adversarial evidence environments to ensure reliability against GEO-style poisoning.

title: Explainable Belief Harmonization Under Dynamic Epistemic Partitions
authors: Jaros{\l}aw A. Chudziak Adam Kostka (warsaw University Of Technology)
abstract: ArXiv:2607.21210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing approaches to multi-agent belief combination have established mature foundations for combining uncertain beliefs under common assumptions: consensus methods use iterative averaging, logic-based methods resolve conflicting knowledge bases, and epistemic logic analyzes agents' information states. Typically, these approaches assume that the structure determining what each agent can represent remains fixed. However, in many scenarios, agents gain or lose observational capacity during execution, and what was once admissible may become structurally impossible. This paper presents a formal framework for handling such runtime changes in epistemic partitions over continuous belief profiles. A hybrid approach exploits the advantages of answer set programming in elaboration tolerance, declarative integrity constraints, and explanations, with the numerical flexibility of Python. The framework applies to domains where agents operate at heterogeneous and possibly changing levels of resolution, and provides formal guarantees of admissibility preservation under refinement, unique mass-preserving repair under coarsening, and explanation completeness. Evaluation across 100 randomly generated topology changes confirms complete violation detection and explanation coverage.
tldr: A framework for belief harmonization under dynamic epistemic partitions using answer set programming and Python.
